title: If cetera were Rome's necessary rites, Paul would already have given the Corinthians all needful
source_text: XIII. Sed, quod majorem vim habet, & adversario potest os obstruere, si per caetera illa, quorum Paulus ordinationem in aliud tempus differt, intelligantur ea quae sentiunt Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae, nempe, sacrificium altaris, ordinatio ministrorum, & alia de Sacramentorum materia & forma, tum quaedam necessaria nondum fuerunt Corinthiis tradita, quum Apostolus hanc epistolam scriberet. Dicunt enim Pontificii sua haec esse in primis necessaria. Sed omnia necessaria Corinthiis abunde ab Apostolo tradita fuerant prius quam hanc epistolam ad illos mitteret, ut patet ex epistolae hujus capite primo, ubi Paulus dicit Corinthios in omnibus divites factos fuisse in Christo, in omni verbo, & in omni scientia. Et capite decimo quinto affirmat Evangelium quod praedicaverat Corinthiis, quod acceperant, & in quo stabant, ejusmodi esse, ut per illud servarentur, siquidem illud retinerent, qua ratione ipsis praedicaverat. Unde manifestum est Apostolum integram & perfectam doctrinam illis antea tradidisse neque quicquam eos celasse quod ad salutem & fidem necessarium judicaret. Igitur oportet, ut, vel Pontificii concedant suas illas traditiones de sacrificio altaris & Sacramentorum materia & forma necessarias non esse, vel agnoscant, non ad illa pertinere, quae Paulus, quum scriberet Corinthiis, nondum tradiderat, sed in posterum se apud ipsos dispositurum esse pollicebatur.
pass_a_gloss: But what has greater force, and can stop the adversary's mouth, if by those remaining things whose arrangement Paul puts off to another time are understood the things which the Doctors of the Roman Church think, namely, the sacrifice of the altar, the ordination of ministers, and other things concerning the matter and form of the Sacraments, then certain necessary things had not yet been delivered to the Corinthians when the Apostle was writing this epistle. For the Pontificians say these things of theirs are among the first necessities. But all things necessary had been abundantly delivered to the Corinthians by the Apostle before he sent this epistle to them, as is clear from the first chapter of this epistle, where Paul says the Corinthians had been made rich in everything in Christ, in every word, and in all knowledge. And in the fifteenth chapter he affirms that the Gospel which he had preached to the Corinthians, which they had received, and in which they stood, was of such a kind that through it they would be saved, if indeed they held it fast, in the way he had preached it to them. Whence it is manifest that the Apostle had before delivered to them an entire and perfect doctrine and had hidden from them nothing which he judged necessary to salvation and faith. Therefore it is necessary either that the Pontificians concede that those traditions of theirs concerning the sacrifice of the altar and the matter and form of the Sacraments are not necessary, or that they acknowledge that they do not pertain to those things which Paul, when he was writing to the Corinthians, had not yet delivered, but promised he would arrange among them later.
pass_b_english: Retorsion: if cetera meant altar-sacrifice and sacrament forms, those were still missing when Paul wrote.
But Rome calls those first necessities — while 1 Cor 1 and 15 say the Corinthians already had every word, knowledge, and saving Gospel.
Paul had given a complete faith-doctrine; he hid nothing needful.
So either those Roman traditions are not necessary, or they are not what Paul postponed.
